gist: Anthony Pompliano talks with Tilman Holloway and Andrew Parish of Arch Public about a Cold Card hardware-wallet failure that cost roughly 5,000 holders about $100 million in Bitcoin, arguing it accelerates a structural migration of Bitcoin holdings from DIY self-custody into ETFs and institutional custody while Bitcoin's price barely moved. They then extend the argument to leverage and predation in markets (the Leopold hedge fund blow-up, Citadel, JP Morgan/First Republic), the rise of agentic retail trading, and an out-of-consensus thesis that Apple, not the model labs, captures the durable revenue from AI.

themes.theme: Cold Card failure and the self-custody trust stack

insights.claim: A Cold Card hardware-wallet entropy failure cost roughly 5,000 of Bitcoin's most technical holders about $100 million, and the victims were users who followed accepted best practice rather than careless holders.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano and Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: The loss vector was the wallet vendor's software, not user error, so any risk model that treats hardware self-custody as counterparty-free is mispriced.
insights.quote: 5,000 plus people who are the most hardcore believers who had $100 million of Bitcoin taken from them

insights.claim: Hardware self-custody is not trustless: the holder is trusting the hardware manufacturer, its firmware updates, and its ability to interact with the chain, a dependency most self-custody users never priced.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: Reframes hardware wallets as a vendor-risk product, which favors audited multisig and insured institutional custody over single-vendor devices.
insights.quote: you're you're trusting a hardware provider at the end of the day. You're trusting the for firmware updates that they're giving you.

insights.claim: The maximalist community's proposed fix to the entropy failure was generating one's own randomness with 100 manual dice rolls rather than moving coins to an exchange or ETF, which the Arch Public guests call unworkable for anyone outside the developer community.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: If the community's own remedy is impractical at scale, retail self-custody share shrinks by default and custodial/ETF share grows.
insights.quote: I'm not rolling a hundred dice and I consider myself to be somewhat of a seasoned veteran in the space.

insights.claim: Multisig and collaborative-custody providers including Casa and Unchained responded to the Cold Card failure by offering migration help rather than gloating, signaling that the self-custody market restructures toward multi-key providers rather than disappearing.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Watch multisig custody providers as the direct share-gainers from single-device wallet failures.

insights.claim: Crypto's custody sector still lacks standardized insurance: Coinbase and BitGo carry coverage in the range of $5 million for events of this type, which the guests argue is inadequate relative to aggregate assets held.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: Custody insurance capacity is a structural gap and a business opportunity; it is also a reason institutions still discount crypto custody.
insights.quote: they have insurance coverage for these types of events like $5 million of insurance

themes.theme: Capital rotation into ETFs and institutional custody

insights.claim: Andrew Parish predicts Bitcoin ETF inflows will show a measurable uptick 3, 6 and 9 months after the Cold Card incident as holders who became uncomfortable with cold storage migrate their coins.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: A tradable, testable call: track spot Bitcoin ETF net flows over the next three quarters against the incident date.
insights.quote: 3 months 6 months 9 months out you'll see just an uptick in inflows across Bitcoin ETFs because people are still moving money from spots that they've now become a little bit uncomfortable with

insights.claim: Institutional spot Bitcoin ETF custody runs roughly 19 to 20 layers deep in security and risk controls according to Bitwise's Matt Hougan, a standard the guests contrast with dice-roll entropy generation.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: Gives ETF issuers a concrete marketing and diligence edge over DIY custody in the post-hack narrative.
insights.quote: It's like 19 to 20 layers deep of security, risk measures, custody at, you know, just huge levels.

insights.claim: High-net-worth investors will not accept the personal liability of self-custody for the same reason they hire pilots and asset managers, so professional custody is the natural end state for large Bitcoin balances.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: Implies wealth-management channels, not wallets, are where large Bitcoin allocations will be sourced and serviced.
insights.quote: I want a ne single neck to choke. Show me a neck that I can choke.

insights.claim: Andrew Parish frames the correct Bitcoin allocation model on the analogy of a wealthy household holding roughly 2% of assets in a home safe and the rest at UBS, Morgan Stanley or JP Morgan, implying self-custody should be a small operational slice rather than the whole position.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: A concrete allocation heuristic advisors can use to size self-custody versus custodial Bitcoin holdings.

insights.claim: Large institutions do not view Bitcoin as a monetary revolution but as one competing wrapper among many, sizing it at roughly 2% to 5% portfolio exposure.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: Caps the realistic institutional bid: allocation decisions will be made on wrapper cost and access, not on ideology.
insights.quote: they don't look at Bitcoin as being the greatest asset that's ever been created. They look at it as a competing rapper now.

themes.theme: Bitcoin price resilience as the real signal

insights.claim: Bitcoin moved less than about 1% on news of a $100 million cold storage hack, which the guests treat as the more important market signal than the custody failure itself.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: Demand depth is absorbing idiosyncratic shocks; sellers of volatility and dip-buyers get confirmation the marginal holder base has changed.
insights.quote: a positive to this is that Bitcoin didn't move more than about 1% on this whole thing

insights.claim: Bitcoin absorbing both repeated Saylor-related announcements described as another version of selling Bitcoin and a nine-figure hack without moving indicates the market has bottomed near the top of the prior cycle.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: A bullish structural read: if the prior cycle top is now the floor, drawdown risk is being repriced upward from here.
insights.quote: we've bottomed. We've bottom at at effectively the top of the last cycle. And so, where we go from here is probably extraordinary.

themes.theme: Leverage, predation and the Leopold blow-up

insights.claim: The Leopold hedge fund blow-up followed the classic pattern of a leveraged book being deliberately hunted, with pressure on specific names and a rumored Citadel-sourced surprise rate-hike narrative preceding a Ken Griffin phone call, though the fund reportedly retains a couple billion dollars.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Concentrated, levered books in crowded AI names are targetable; position sizing and disclosure of leverage are the risk variables to watch.

insights.claim: Pompliano raises the unresolved question of whether the hunting of leveraged positions is now being executed by AI agents explicitly tasked to seek out and break specific funds, rather than by humans or static algorithms.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: If agentic predation of levered books is real, it shortens the time from stress to liquidation and raises tail risk for crowded trades.
insights.quote: they basically are like unoffensively unleashing agents to go and hunt out positions like that

insights.claim: The same asset-capture dynamic Citadel runs in trading is run by JP Morgan in banking, illustrated by JP Morgan absorbing First Republic's hundreds of billions in wealth-management assets after it collapsed in about a week roughly two and a half years ago.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: Distress events reliably transfer assets to the balance-sheet holder with liquidity; own the consolidators, not the consolidated.
insights.quote: he who holds the gold makes the rules

insights.claim: Ken Griffin's edge in a resurfaced interview was being the only bidder able to mobilize over a weekend to value a distressed book, showing that speed of mobilization, not just capital, is the source of distressed-asset returns.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: Operational readiness is the moat in distressed situations; firms without weekend mobilization capacity systematically lose those deals.
insights.quote: when you're the only bidder on something that's going bust on Monday morning, that's that's a good spot to be in

insights.claim: Tilman Holloway argues leveraged retail and fund traders are structurally the sucker at the table because counterparties with infinite bankrolls profit from prolonged irrationality, which is why Buffett-style compounding without leverage remains the only reliable path to exponential returns.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: Argues against levered expressions of high-conviction views; the edge is survival and compounding, not maximizing notional.
insights.quote: the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent

insights.claim: More than 70% of volume in every market is already automated algorithmic trading, so agentic trading is not new to markets, only newly available to retail.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: The investable change is distribution of automation to retail, not the automation itself; brokers with agent products capture that shift.
insights.quote: if you look at the volume of every market, 70 plus% of it is automated trading is is algorithmic trading

insights.claim: Robinhood reports about 100,000 accounts signed up for agentic trading tools against a user base of roughly 100 million-plus, meaning under 1% penetration of retail agentic trading today.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Quantifies how early retail agentic trading is and gives a baseline adoption metric to track at Robinhood and Coinbase.

insights.claim: Arch Public's product thesis is that retail cannot harvest volatility manually because reacting to moves is too slow, so pre-set programmatic traps for dip accumulation and profit-taking are the only scalable way to do it across assets and timeframes.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: Frames automation's real value as pre-committed execution rather than prediction, the pitch that will drive retail agent adoption.
insights.quote: harvesting volatility is just having traps set or automated, you know, trades programmatically waiting for the volatility or for those conditions to be met versus reacting to them

themes.theme: AI model economics: hardware, data and the Apple revenue thesis

insights.claim: Andrew Parish's out-of-consensus call is that Apple wins AI on revenue rather than model share, because roughly 4 billion iPhones plus App Store toll-taking, biometric authentication and cross-app visibility give it a moat that survives collapsing model pricing.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: An explicit long-Apple-as-AI-winner thesis that pays off if model-layer pricing commoditizes while distribution rents persist.
insights.quote: There's 4 billion iPhones that people are using. That is that's a moat. That is a meaningful moat.

insights.claim: AI subscription pricing will follow the path of packaged software and operating systems toward near-zero as labs compete for universal consumer adoption, with only enterprise contracts staying juicy for a while.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: Bearish for consumer-subscription-dependent model labs and bullish for whoever owns the distribution layer and enterprise deployment.

insights.claim: Andrew Parish reads OpenAI and Anthropic both pushing back their IPOs as evidence that pricing pressure is creating balance-sheet items they are not eager to disclose in a filing.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: Speculative but actionable framing: treat delayed AI-lab IPOs as a margin-pressure signal for the whole model layer.
insights.quote: they both pushed back their IPOs. There's a reason for that.

insights.claim: Competitive advantage in AI will come from proprietary data quality, user experience and owning hardware and compute, not from model intelligence, because models are commoditizing toward whatever gets the task done cheapest.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: Directs capital toward compute owners and vertical data-owning applications rather than the frontier-model layer.
insights.quote: that's not going to be how smart is your model. That's going to be how good is the data that you're feeding it that is proprietary

insights.claim: Palantir's CTO argues public AI benchmarks are irrelevant because open-weight models tuned with custom harnesses and proprietary data pipelines can outperform frontier models on the specific task at hand.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Undercuts benchmark-driven narratives that support frontier-lab valuations and supports open-weight adoption in enterprise.

insights.claim: AI adoption is only in the first or second inning because roughly 90% of people still do not use any AI model, defaulting to Google or asking a friend.
insights.speaker: Andrew Parish
insights.so_what: Implies the consumer AI TAM is still nearly untapped and that current usage-based valuations rest on a narrow user base.
insights.quote: 90% of people still don't use this

insights.claim: Tilman Holloway's stated AI portfolio approach is to bet on the whole space rather than one company and, if narrowing, to go down the hardware supply chain, citing parabolic growth in SanDisk as an example of component demand repricing.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: A basket-plus-supply-chain construction: pick the picks-and-shovels layer where demand is physical and measurable.
insights.quote: it's just better to bet on the space as a whole. And if you really want to get nitty-gritty, you look at the supply chain of that space and you start betting on the hardware providers.

insights.claim: The largest untapped AI opportunity is applying AI to the most pen-and-paper legacy industries and selling that solution to incumbents, which Tilman Holloway calls the hardest delta to capture but the largest.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: Points venture and growth capital toward vertical AI in unglamorous sectors rather than horizontal model or tooling plays.
insights.quote: I'd be looking at the most pen and paper industry I could find.

insights.claim: Tilman Holloway argues the US government has an obligation to print a large amount of money to invest in AI technology, an implicit call for fiscal expansion funding the buildout.
insights.speaker: Tilman Holloway
insights.so_what: If state-financed AI buildout becomes policy, it supports both the hardware complex and the debasement case for Bitcoin.
insights.quote: I think the US has an obligation to its people to print a lot of money and invest in this technology.
